activities.caption: one line of the income statement is wrong
activities.name: fmIncomeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this worked income statement is wrong. Find it.
lines: COGS at 12 per unit: 1,200,000 — gross profit 800,000 (40%)
Interest 32,000 on 400,000 of debt at 8%; tax at 25%; net income 201,000
config.why: Every figure below a driver is a formula, and the formula says 300,000 — the model's whole virtue is that no number is typed in unexplained.

activities.anchor: Working-capital items are driven off the income statement by days
activities.caption: build the balance sheet block, driver by driver
activities.name: fmWorkingOrder

config.prompt: Build the balance sheet block in the model's own order:
items: Add cash 100,000 and fixed assets 650,000 — total assets 1,100,000
Equity comes out at 530,000 — rolled forward from net income, never typed in
config.why: Forecast every asset and liability from drivers, choose the financing, and let cash be the plug — the balance check becomes the model's lie detector.

activities.anchor: The professional technique is to forecast every asset
activities.caption: the matching principle — which instrument funds which asset
activities.name: fmMatchingBuckets

config.prompt: The matching principle — file each financing need:

items.label: a machine earning returns over ten years

config.why: Short-term working-capital gaps want revolving credit; long-lived assets want term debt or equity — never an overdraft that can be called in a bad month.

activities.anchor: cash conversion cycle is the summary statistic
activities.caption: call the magnitude — cash locked in operations
activities.name: fmCccEstimate

config.prompt: In this model firm, how many days of cash are locked in operations (receivables + inventory − payables days)?
config.why: 37 days of receivables + 46 days of inventory − 37 days of payables = 46 days — about 250,000 of cash locked in operations on 2,000,000 of sales.
config.context: That is why the firm is profitable and still one late-paying customer away from an overdraft.

activities.anchor: Fast-growing firms die of it most often
activities.caption: true or false — profit versus cash
activities.name: fmProfitJudge

statements.s: A profitable company cannot run out of money.
statements.why: Profit is an accounting result; insolvency is a date on which the cash balance goes negative.

statements.s: Fast-growing firms die of overtrading — every extra sale buys inventory and receivables before the cash arrives.
statements.why: That is why the weekly cash forecast sits at the centre of the model, not the profit line.

statements.s: The model firm books 2,000,000 of revenue while only ~1,800,000 has been collected — and is still solvent.
statements.why: Accrual accounting spreads events across the periods that cash ignores.

statements.s: Insolvency is a matter of totals, not dates.
statements.why: It is a matter of dates — which is why cash forecasts are built weekly in practice.

activities.caption: read the dashboard — ratio to value
activities.name: fmRatioMatch

config.prompt: Pair each ratio with this model firm's value:
config.why: ROCE comfortably above any plausible WACC means value creation; DuPont then splits the 37.9% ROE into margin (10.1%) × turnover (1.82) × leverage (2.08).

activities.anchor: a 66.7% profit hit from a 10% price move
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the price-cut stress test
activities.name: fmPriceEstimate

config.prompt: Cut price 10% (to 18) with volume unchanged. What percentage hit does this model firm's EBIT take?
config.why: EBIT falls from 300,000 to 100,000 — the discount strips contribution margin from every unit while opex stays fixed. A 10% volume gain instead lifts EBIT only 26.7%.
config.context: Price dominates volume in this business: the elasticity arithmetic of a discount is brutal.

activities.anchor: and the headline is a lie
activities.caption: fill the blanks — split the variance
activities.name: fmVarianceCloze

config.text: Forecast 100,000 units at 20; actual 105,000 at 19 — the headline gap is −5,000, which hides the real story. Split it: the volume effect at budget price is %%0%%, the price effect on actual volume is %%1%% — and the sales team's over-delivery was given away on price.
